mn119:1.2: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthi in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
mn119:2.1: Then a number of bhikkhus were sitting in the assembly hall where they had met together on return from their alms-round after their meal was over. Meanwhile it was being said among them:
mn119:2.2: ‘It is wonderful, friends, it is marvellous,
mn119:2.3: how mindfulness of the body has been said by the Blessed One who knows and sees, Arahant and Fully Enlightened, to be of great fruit, of great benefit when developed and repeatedly practised!’
mn119:2.4: Then their talk meanwhile was left unfinished for the Blessed One rose from meditation now when it was evening, and he came to the assembly hall and sat down on a seat made ready.
mn119:2.5: When he had done so, he addressed the bhikkhus thus:
mn119:2.6: ‘For what talk are you gathered here together now, bhikkhus? And what was your talk meanwhile which was left unfinished?’
mn119:2.7: ‘Here, venerable sir, we were sitting in the assembly hall where we had met together on return from our alms-round after our meal. Meanwhile it was being said amongst us:
mn119:2.8: “It is wonderful, friends, it is marvellous,
mn119:2.9: how mindfulness of the body has been said by the Blessed One who knows and sees, Arahant and Fully Enlightened, to be of great fruit, of great benefit when developed and repeatedly practised!”
mn119:2.10: This was our talk meanwhile, venerable sir, which was left unfinished, for then the Blessed One arrived.’
mn119:3.1: ‘And how developed, bhikkhus, how repeatedly practised is mindfulness of the body of great fruit, of great benefit?
mn119:4.1: ‘Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu gone to the forest or to the root of a tree or to an empty hut, sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, established mindfulness before him,
mn119:4.2: just mindful he breathes in, mindful he breathes out.
mn119:4.3: ‘Breathing in long, he understands: “I breathe in long”; breathing out long, he understands: “I breathe out long”.
mn119:4.4: Breathing in short, he understands: “I breathe in short”; breathing out short, he understands: “I breathe out short”.
mn119:4.5: He trains thus: “I shall breathe in experiencing a whole body”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe out experiencing a whole body”.
mn119:4.6: He trains thus: “I shall breathe in tranquillizing the body process”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe out tranquillizing the bodily process”. Just as a skilled turner or his apprentice, when making a long turn understands: “I make a long turn”; or when making a short turn understands: “I make a short turn”; so too, breathing in long, he understands: “I breathe in long”; breathing out long, he understands: “I breathe out long”; breathing in short, he understands: “I breathe in short”; breathing out short, he understands: “I breathe out short”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe in experiencing a whole body”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe out experiencing a whole body”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe in tranquillizing the bodily process”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe out tranquillizing the bodily process”.
mn119:4.7: ‘As he abides thus diligent, ardent and self-controlled, his memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned;
mn119:4.8: with their abandoning his mind becomes settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.
mn119:4.9: That is how a bhikkhu develops mindfulness of the body.
mn119:5.1: ‘Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu when walking, understands: “I walk”; when standing, understands: “I stand”; when sitting, understands: “I sit”; when lying down, understands: “I am lying down”;
mn119:5.2: or however his body is disposed he understands accordingly.
mn119:5.3: As he abides thus diligent, ardent and self-controlled, his memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned;
mn119:5.4: with their abandoning his mind becomes settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.
mn119:5.5: That is how a bhikkhu develops mindfulness of the body.
mn119:6.1: ‘Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who acts in full awareness when moving to and fro, who acts in full awareness when looking at and away, who acts in full awareness when flexing and extending, who acts in full awareness when wearing the patched cloak, bowl and robes, who acts in full awareness when feeding, drinking and supping, who acts in full awareness when evacuating the bowels and making water, who acts in full awareness when walking, standing, sitting, falling asleep, waking up, talking, and keeping silent.
mn119:6.2: As he abides thus diligent, ardent and self-controlled, his memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned;
mn119:6.3: with their abandoning his mind becomes settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.
mn119:6.4: That is how a bhikkhu develops mindfulness of the body.
mn119:7.1: ‘Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu reviews this same body up from the soles of the feet and down from the top of the hair as full of many kinds of filth, thus:
mn119:7.2: “In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs, bowels, entrails, gorge, dung, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil of the joints and urine”.
mn119:7.3: ‘Just as though there were a bag with an opening at both (ends) full of many sorts of grain such as
mn119:7.4: hill rice, red rice, beans, peas, millet and white rice,
mn119:7.5: and a man with (clear) eyes had opened it and were reviewing it thus:
mn119:7.6: “This is hill rice, this is red rice, these are beans, these are peas, this is millet, this is white rice”,
mn119:7.7: so too, a bhikkhu reviews this same body up from the soles of the feet and down from the top of the hair as full of many kinds of filth,
mn119:7.8: “In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs, bowels, entrails, gorge, dung, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil of the joints and urine”.
mn119:7.9: As he abides thus diligent, ardent and self-controlled, his memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned;
mn119:7.10: with their abandoning his mind becomes settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.
mn119:7.11: That is how a bhikkhu develops mindfulness of the body.
mn119:8.1: ‘Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu reviews this same body however it is placed (consisting of) elements, thus:
mn119:8.2: “In this body there are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element”.
mn119:8.3: ‘Just as though a skilled butcher or his apprentice had killed a cow and were seated at the four crossroads with it cut up into pieces;
mn119:8.4: so too, however it is placed, however disposed, a bhikkhu reviews this same body,
mn119:8.5: “In this body there are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element”.
mn119:8.6: As he abides thus diligent, ardent and self-controlled, his memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned;
mn119:8.7: with their abandoning his mind becomes settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.
mn119:8.8: That is how a bhikkhu develops mindfulness of the body.
mn119:9.1: ‘Again, bhikkhus, as though a bhikkhu here were looking at bodily remains thrown on a charnel ground one day dead, two days dead, three days dead, bloated, livid, and oozing matter,
mn119:9.2: he compares this same body with it, thus:
mn119:9.3: “This body too is of such a nature, it will be like that, it is not exempt from that”.
mn119:9.4: As he abides thus diligent, ardent and self-controlled, his memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned;
mn119:9.5: with their abandoning his mind becomes settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.
mn119:9.6: That is how a bhikkhu develops mindfulness of the body.
mn119:10.1: ‘Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu judges this same body as though he were looking at bodily remains thrown on a charnel ground, being devoured by crows, kites, vultures, herons, dogs, tigers, leopards, jackals, and the multitudinous kinds of worms,
mn119:10.2: he compares this same body with it, thus:
mn119:10.3: “This body too is of such a nature, it will be like that, it is not exempt from that”.
mn119:10.4: As he abides thus diligent, ardent and self-controlled, his memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned; with their abandoning his mind becomes settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.
mn119:10.5: That is how a bhikkhu develops mindfulness of the body.
mn119:11-14.1: ‘Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu judges this same body as though he were looking at bodily remains thrown on a charnel ground, a skeleton with flesh and blood held together with sinews,
mn119:11-14.2: a fleshless skeleton smeared with blood and held together with sinews,
mn119:11-14.3: a skeleton without flesh and blood held together with sinews,
mn119:11-14.4: bones without sinews scattered in all directions: here a hand-bone, there a foot-bone, there a shin-bone, there a thigh-bone, there a hip-bone, there a back-bone, there a rib-bone, there a breast-bone, there an arm-bone, there a shoulder-bone, there a neck-bone, there a jaw-bone, there a tooth-bone, there the skull,
mn119:11-14.5: he compares this same body with it, thus:
mn119:11-14.6: “This body too is of such a nature, it will be like that, it is not exempt from that”.
mn119:11-14.7: As he abides thus diligent, ardent and self-controlled, his memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned; with their abandoning his mind becomes settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.
mn119:11-14.8: That is how a bhikkhu develops mindfulness of the body.
mn119:15-17.1: ‘Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu judges this same body as though he were looking at bodily remains thrown on a charnel ground,
mn119:15-17.2: bones bleached white, the colour of shells,
mn119:15-17.3: bones heaped up, more than a year old,
mn119:15-17.4: bones rotted and crumbled to dust,
mn119:15-17.5: he compares this same body with it, thus:
mn119:15-17.6: “This body too is of such a nature, it will be like that, it is not exempt from that”.
mn119:15-17.7: As he abides thus diligent, ardent and self-controlled, his memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned;
mn119:15-17.8: with their abandoning his mind becomes settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.
mn119:15-17.9: That is how a bhikkhu develops mindfulness of the body.
mn119:18.1: ‘Again, bhikkhus, quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unprofitable dhammas, he enters upon and abides in the first jhana which is accompanied by initial and sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of seclusion.
mn119:18.2: ‘He makes happiness and pleasure born of seclusion drench, steep, fill and extend throughout his whole body, so that there is nothing of his whole body to which the happiness and pleasure born of seclusion do not extend.
mn119:18.3: Just as a skilled bath man or bath man’s apprentice heaps bath powder in a metal basin and, sprinkling it gradually with water, kneads it up till the moisture wets his ball of bath powder, soaks it, and extends over it within and without though it does not itself become liquid,
mn119:18.4: so too, a bhikkhu makes happiness and pleasure born of seclusion drench, steep, fill, and extend throughout his whole body, so that there is nothing of his whole body to which the happiness and pleasure born of seclusion do not extend.
mn119:18.5: ‘As he abides thus diligent, ardent and self-controlled, his memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned;
mn119:18.6: with their abandoning his mind becomes settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.
mn119:18.7: That is how a bhikkhu develops mindfulness of the body.
mn119:19.1: ‘Again, bhikkhus, with the stilling of initial and sustained application he enters upon and abides in the second jhāna, which has self-confidence and singleness of mind, without initial application and without sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of concentration.
mn119:19.2: ‘He makes happiness and pleasure born of concentration drench, steep, fill and extend throughout this body, and there is nothing of his whole body to which the happiness and pleasure born of concentration do not extend.
mn119:19.3: Just as though there were a lake whose waters welled up (from below), having no inflow from east, west, north or south, nor yet replenished from time to time by the skies with showers, then the cool fount of water welling up in the lake would make the cool water drench, steep, fill and extend throughout the lake, and there would be nothing of the whole lake to which the cool water did not extend,
mn119:19.4: so, too, the bhikkhu makes happiness and pleasure born of concentration drench, steep, fill and extend throughout this body, so that there is nothing of his whole body to which the happiness and pleasure born of concentration do not extend.
mn119:19.5: ‘As he abides thus diligent, ardent and self-controlled, his memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned; with their abandoning his mind becomes settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.
mn119:19.6: That is how a bhikkhu develops mindfulness of the body.
mn119:20.1: ‘Again, bhikkhus, with the fading as well of happiness he abides in equanimity, and mindful and fully aware, still feeling pleasure with the body, he enters upon and abides in the third jhāna, on account of which the Noble Ones announce: “He has a pleasant abiding who has equanimity and is mindful.”
mn119:20.2: ‘He makes pleasure divested of happiness drench, steep, fill and extend throughout this body, and there is nothing of his whole body to which the pleasure divested of happiness does not extend.
mn119:20.3: Just as, in a water-lily pond or a white lotus pond or a red lotus pond some water-lilies or white lotuses or red lotuses are born under the water, grow under the water, do not stand up out of the water, flourish immersed under the water, and cool water drenches, steeps, fill and extends throughout them, to their tips and to their roots, and there is nothing of the whole of those water-lilies, those white lotuses, those red lotuses, to which the cool water does not extend,
mn119:20.4: so too, the bhikkhu makes pleasure divested of happiness drench, steep, fill and extend throughout this body, and there is nothing of his whole body to which pleasure divested of happiness does not extend.
mn119:20.5: ‘As he abides thus diligent, ardent and self-controlled, his memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned; with their abandoning his mind becomes settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness and concentrated.
mn119:20.6: That is how a bhikkhu develops mindfulness of the body.
mn119:21.1: ‘Again, bhikkhus, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure, and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.
mn119:21.2: ‘He sits with pure bright mind extending over this body, and there is nothing of his whole body to which the pure bright mind does not extend.
mn119:21.3: Just as though a man were sitting clothed from head to foot in white cloth, and there were nothing of his whole body to which the white cloth did not extend,
mn119:21.4: so too, the bhikkhu sits with a pure bright mind extending over this body, and there is nothing of his whole body to which the pure bright mind does not extend.
mn119:21.5: ‘As he abides thus diligent, ardent and self-controlled, his memories and intentions based on the household life are abandoned;
mn119:21.6: with their abandoning his mind becomes settled in himself, quieted, brought to singleness, and concentrated.
mn119:21.7: That is how a bhikkhu develops mindfulness of the body.
mn119:22.1: ‘When anyone has developed and repeatedly practised mindfulness of the body, he has included whatever profitable dhammas there are that partake of true knowledge.
mn119:22.2: ‘Just as anyone who extends his mind over the great ocean has included whatever streams there are that flow into the ocean,
mn119:22.3: so too, when anyone has developed and repeatedly practised mindfulness of the body, he has included whatever profitable dhammas there are that partake of true knowledge.
mn119:23.1: ‘When anyone has not developed or repeatedly practised mindfulness of the body, Māra finds an opportunity and a support in him.
mn119:23.2: ‘Suppose a man were to throw a heavy stone ball at a heap of wet clay;
mn119:23.4: would that heavy stone ball find an entry into that heap of wet clay?’
mn119:23.6: ‘So too, bhikkhus, when anyone has not developed or repeatedly practised mindfulness of the body, Māra finds an opportunity and a support in him.
mn119:24.1: ‘Suppose there were a dry sapless piece of wood
mn119:24.2: and man came with an upper fire-stick, thinking:
mn119:24.3: “I shall light a fire, I shall produce heat”;
mn119:24.5: would the man light a fire and produce heat by rubbing the dry sapless piece of wood with an upper fire-stick?’
mn119:24.7: ‘So too, bhikkhus, when anyone has not developed or repeatedly practised mindfulness of the body, Māra finds an opportunity and a support in him.
mn119:25.1: ‘Suppose there were a hollow empty water pot standing on a stand
mn119:25.2: and a man came with a load of water;
mn119:25.4: would he be able to pour water into it?’
mn119:25.6: ‘So too, bhikkhus, when anyone has not developed or repeatedly practised mindfulness of the body, Māra finds an opportunity and a support in him.
mn119:26.1: ‘When anyone has developed and repeatedly practised mindfulness of the body, Māra finds no opportunity or support in him.
mn119:26.2: ‘Suppose a man were to throw a light ball of string at a door-panel all made of heartwood;
mn119:26.4: would that light ball of string find an entry into that door-panel all made of heartwood?’
mn119:26.6: ‘So too, bhikkhus, when anyone has developed and repeatedly practised mindfulness of the body, Māra finds no opportunity or support in him.
mn119:27.1: ‘Suppose there were a wet sappy piece of wood,
mn119:27.2: and a man came with an upper fire-stick, thinking,
mn119:27.3: “I shall light a fire, I shall produce heat”;
mn119:27.5: would the man light a fire and produce heat by taking the upper fire-stick and rubbing the wet sappy piece of wood with it?’
mn119:27.7: ‘So too, bhikkhus, when anyone has developed and repeatedly practised mindfulness of the body, Māra finds no opportunity or support in him.
mn119:28.1: ‘Suppose there were a water pot full of water, brimming so that crows could drink out of it, standing on a stand,
mn119:28.2: and man came with a load of water;
mn119:28.4: would he be able to pour water into it?’
mn119:28.6: ‘So too, bhikkhus, when anyone has developed and repeatedly practised mindfulness of the body, Māra finds no opportunity or support in him.
mn119:29.1: ‘When anyone has developed and repeatedly practised mindfulness of the body, (then) he attains the ability to be a witness, through realization by direct knowledge, of any dhamma realizable by direct knowledge to which he inclines his mind, whenever there is opportunity.
mn119:29.2: ‘Suppose there were a water pot full of water, brimming so that crows could drink out of it, standing on a stand,
mn119:29.3: then as soon as a strong man tipped it would water come (from it) each time?’
mn119:29.5: ‘So too, bhikkhus, when anyone has developed and repeatedly practised mindfulness of the body, (then) he attains the ability to be a witness, through realization by direct knowledge, of any dhamma realizable by direct knowledge to which he inclines his mind, whenever there is opportunity.’
mn119:30.1: ‘Suppose there were a square pond on a level piece of ground, surrounded by an embankment, full of water, brimming so that crows could drink out of it,
mn119:30.2: then as soon as a strong man loosened the embankment would water come (from it) each time?’
mn119:30.4: ‘So too, bhikkhus, when anyone has developed and repeatedly practised mindfulness of the body, (then) he attains the ability to be a witness, through realization by direct knowledge, of any dhamma realizable by direct knowledge to which he inclines his mind, whenever there is opportunity.’
mn119:31.1: ‘Suppose there were a chariot on even ground at the four cross-roads, harnessed to thoroughbreds, waiting with whips lying ready,
mn119:31.2: so that a skilled trainer, a driver of horses to be tamed, might mount, and taking the reins in his hand, drive out and back by any road in any way he liked,
mn119:31.3: so too, bhikkhus, So too, bhikkhus, when anyone has developed and repeatedly practised mindfulness of the body, (then) he attains the ability to be a witness, through realization by direct knowledge, of any dhamma realizable by direct knowledge to which he inclines his mind, whenever there is opportunity.’
mn119:32.1: ‘When mindfulness of the body is developed, repeatedly practised, made the vehicle, made the basis, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken, these ten rewards may be expected. What ten?
mn119:33.1: ‘He becomes a conqueror of aversion and delight and aversion does not conquer him, and he abides transcending aversion as it arises.
mn119:34.1: ‘He becomes a conqueror of fear and dread, fear and dread do not conquer him, and he abides transcending fear and dread as they arise.
mn119:35.1: ‘He becomes one who bears cold and heat, hunger and thirst and contact with mosquitoes, flies, wind, sun and creeping things, who endures ill-spoken unwelcome words and arisen bodily feelings that are painful, racking, sharp, piercing, disagreeable, distressing, and menacing to life.
mn119:36.1: ‘He becomes one who obtains at will with no trouble and easily the four jhānas which are the higher mind and provide a pleasant abiding here and now.
mn119:37.1: ‘He wields the various kinds of supernormal success … (as in Sutta 77, para. 31) … even as far as the world of the Divinity (Brahmā).
mn119:38.1: ‘With the heavenly ear element … (Sutta 77, para. 32) … far as well as near.
mn119:39.1: ‘He encompasses with his mind the minds of other beings, of other persons, and understands them:
mn119:39.2: he understands a mind with lust as a mind with lust,
mn119:39.3: and a mind without lust as a mind without lust;
mn119:39.4: a mind with hate as a mind with hate,
mn119:39.5: and a mind without hate as a mind without hate;
mn119:39.6: a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion,
mn119:39.7: and a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion;
mn119:39.8: a contracted mind as a contracted mind,
mn119:39.9: and a distracted mind as a distracted mind;
mn119:39.10: an exalted mind as an exalted mind,
mn119:39.11: and an unexalted mind as an unexalted mind;
mn119:39.12: a surpassed mind as a surpassed mind,
mn119:39.13: and an unsurpassed mind as an unsurpassed mind;
mn119:39.14: a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind,
mn119:39.15: and an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind;
mn119:39.16: a liberated mind as a liberated mind,
mn119:39.17: and the unliberated mind as unliberated.
mn119:40.1: ‘He recollects his manifold past life … (Sutta 77, para. 34) … with its details and particulars.
mn119:41.1: ‘With the heavenly eyesight … (Sutta 77, para. 35) … according to their kammas.
mn119:42.1: ‘By realization himself with direct knowledge here and now, he enters upon and abides in the deliverance of the heart and the deliverance by understanding that are taint-free with exhaustion of taints.
mn119:43.1: ‘When mindfulness of the body is developed, repeatedly practised, made the vehicle, made the basis, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken, these ten rewards may be expected.’
mn119:43.2: This is what the Blessed One said.
mn119:43.3: The bhikkhus were satisfied and they delighted in the Blessed One’s words.
